implement: legion-worker: the phase charter for this repository — the commit, push and handoff rules, and references/pr-body.md for the shape of the proof line and the proof array, which this plan's per-slice surfaces feed; references/default-branch-check.md before the push.

dispatch-first, then dispatch: every write this phase makes to the issue (a message, a comment, an ask for the hand-applied grant the database slice needs) goes through them, and dispatch-first's search rule applies before any new ask.

ce-simplify-code: the simplify pass over the settled diff before completion, which matters here because the broker slice adds a second grant beside an existing one and duplication between them is the likely defect.
test: legion-worker: references/pr-body.md defines what this deployment counts as a test — the application booted and driven, with CI read for everything static — which is the rule the per-slice surfaces in the plan were chosen against (packages/envoy/scripts/dev-broker.sh, packages/dispatch/e2e, the stage scripts).
dispatch-first, then dispatch: for the tester's own writes to the issue.
review: legion-worker: references/review-threads.md for answering and resolving each thread one at a time, and references/merge-gate.md for the order of the round and the approval of a head by its commit.
dispatch-first, then dispatch: for any review finding that belongs on the issue rather than on the pull request.

findings.finding: F1: a pod's token has no carrier for its project claim — one worker service account covers every project a daemon launches pods for (manifest.go:415, config/kubernetes.go:632-635).
findings.answer: Decision D1: the deployment names one worker service account per project in each daemon's own configuration file, so the broker's map from service account to project and person is correct with no Legion change and no project parameter on the exchange. Recorded as a departure, since the spec reads as though one account could serve several projects.

findings.finding: F2: 'a write that belongs to no project is refused' would stop writes agents make every day, among them an agent uploading a file into its own conversation (routes_table.go:111, owner.go:62-70) and the Stage 4b rig creating its own project.
findings.answer: Decision D2: three classes of write, classed once in the route table — project-owned (must match), session-owned (allowed, because the token names the session), deployment-wide (refused to a project-scoped token). Child G gives the rigs a credential of their own.

findings.finding: F3: 'the session comes from the token' cannot merge before every caller holds such a token; today every bearer names its session in the request body (server.go:669-680) and the daemon names a fabricated one (client.go:304-314).
findings.answer: Decision D5: a body actor may be present and must match the token; a credential that carries no session keeps today's behaviour. Decision D14 keeps the daemon's session name. Section 7 makes this a standing rule rather than a transitional one, and gates Child D on an observed running Dispatch build.

findings.finding: F4: nothing on any client can produce the DPoP proof Dispatch is required to check, and the one proof producer in the tree omits the ath claim (helper/dpop.go:96).
findings.answer: Decision D6: each Dispatch client generates its own key in its own process, exchanges, keeps both in memory, signs each request and renews. Child D builds it in TypeScript and Go. This also answers F11, since no file refresher and no extra process is needed.

findings.finding: F5: the broker cannot register the clients the exchange and introspection need, and the library refuses a public client at introspection (oauthstore/client.go:11-46, client_authentication.go:330-333 against :383-386).
findings.answer: Decisions D7 and D8: the exchanging callers are public clients at the token endpoint; Dispatch is not a client at all, because the introspection route authenticates Dispatch's own Kubernetes token and then calls IntrospectToken (introspect.go:50), which takes no client authentication. The client store grows the registrations the exchange interface needs (handler/rfc8693/client.go:9-47).

findings.finding: F6: 'the broker stops believing an approver's name because of who sent it' has no mechanism, and the obvious ones are near the rule that no sign-in provider lives inside the broker.
findings.answer: Section 3 item 3, sent to the architect with a recommendation: Dispatch signs a short-lived assertion naming the signed-in person and publishes the key that verifies it, and the broker treats it as one more configured issuer. The broker half rides the root slice so the broker is restarted once; the Dispatch half is Child A, and the removal of the shared bearer is Child G. Whether Dispatch may hold a signing key is the person's to answer.

findings.finding: F7: a token that expires mid-connection has no story for the document websocket, which is authorized once at the upgrade (docs/websocket.go:307-325).
findings.answer: Section 3 item 1, sent to the architect: the recommendation is to carry the new credential across the upgrade and close the connection when the token expires or introspection reports it gone. Child A carries it either way.

findings.finding: F8: the document websocket's bearer branch has no production client, so deleting it and implementing it cost very different amounts.
findings.answer: Same decision as F7. Child A names both branches and says which acceptance line is emptied if the architect rules for deletion.

findings.finding: F9: removing the shared token breaks five live rigs and two daemon configuration refusals that tests pin.
findings.answer: Child G is the cutover and lists them: the browser suite mints a personal token it already can (e2e/api.ts:183), the Legion rigs exchange against the broker they already run, the staging-token assertion inverts, and the dispatch_token_file keys and their refusals go with Child D (stage3.go:96-98,557-559; controller.go:143-154).

findings.finding: F10: the Envoy listener half is unsettled — pods already have a non-shared path (cmd/listener/apiauth.go:58-76), panes and dev boxes do not.
findings.answer: Section 3 item 2, sent to the architect: the recommendation is Child F, which gives the listener the same introspection check Dispatch gets, sharing Child A's package.

findings.finding: F11: renewal inside a pod has no process to run in, since the pod shape admits no sidecar (config/kubernetes.go:205-218).
findings.answer: Decision D12: D6 removes the need for any Dispatch file refresher. The only remaining file-refresher question is the database credential, and Child H owns it alone, with the launcher as the one process already in the container.

findings.finding: F12: Dispatch has no way to tell a broker token from a personal token without a round trip.
findings.answer: Decision D9: signed-JSON-web-token shape first, then one indexed lookup in agent_tokens, then introspection with an affirmative cache of a few seconds keyed by the token's hash and never past its expiry. No new prefix and no library change; the per-request cost of each kind is stated.

findings.finding: F13: the project default assignee is a migration, a route, a settings page and a browser test, and the existing chain validates against the people table (issue_assignee.go:37-62).
findings.answer: Child C, which can start at once because it needs no token work. Decision D11 settles the two edges: a signed-in person sets it, and a stale value falls through to nobody rather than refusing the issue.

findings.finding: F14: whoami's answer shape is a contract three live surfaces and an agent tool depend on.
findings.answer: Child A names the shape change and every consumer it reaches: the route index text (routes_table.go:81), the agent tool (dispatch-execute.ts:2656-2663) and the four skill documents that describe the old chain.

findings.finding: F15: the project check needs a per-route resolver and the route table has no such column; some writes need a database read to resolve their project.
findings.answer: Child B classes every mutating row under D2 and gives each class its resolver, which is also where the reads live. The refusal names the project.

findings.finding: F16: ten acceptance lines need machine-checkable restatements, and one is unprovable while the token lifetime is a compiled constant (provider.go:100).
findings.answer: Decision D10 makes the lifetime a setting with the same default, so renewal is proven in seconds. Section 5's table and each child's Proof paragraph give every acceptance line a surface, a command and a negative control.

findings.finding: F17: the spec never says whether a token that names a person satisfies the human-only routes.
findings.answer: Decision D4: it stays a bearer and still gets 403 on those routes. Written down so no reviewer reads 'acts for a person' as 'is that person'.

findings.finding: F18: personal tokens and cookies carry no project, and whether the check applies to them is unstated.
findings.answer: Decision D3: a person's own credentials stay unscoped and cover every project, as today. Scoping them is a column, a route and a control, and is named as outside this tree.

findings.finding: F19: a daemon-launched pane on a dev box has none of the machinery a pod has, and whom it acts for is unstated.
findings.answer: Decision D13 and Child E: the pane is told where the helper's socket is and its session exchanges the machine credential through it, acting for the person who approved that machine.

findings.finding: F20: eleven spec claims are unsupported or superseded, among them the restart window, the connection limit and the question of whether the agent's session client re-reads its URL file.
findings.answer: Section 4 records the superseded cost paragraph as a departure and asks for no window. Child H is written with both branches of the file-reading question specified and settles it with the experiment as its first task. The live-state counts that motivate the issue are not repeated as settled fact anywhere in the plan.

findings.finding: F21: nine pairs of slices that could leave the deployment broken between merges, since each merges and deploys separately and Dispatch deploys by hand.
findings.answer: Section 7 states the five rules that follow from them: the broker deploys first; Legion starts on an observed running Dispatch build; the project and session checks are no-ops for credentials that carry neither; the shared token is removed last; and every broker change rides one announced restart, which is why the root slice also carries the approver assertion.

findings.finding: F22: five questions only the person the work is for can answer.
findings.answer: Two reach the person through the architect, in section 3: whether Dispatch may hold a signing key, and whether a stolen pod token may be exchanged or the exchange must require a live pod. The database slice going first is already the architect's open question. The service-account-to-person names are deployment configuration the person supplies when the deployment change is made. The restart window is dropped: the flag needs none, and the database is moving to an instance of its own.

findings.finding: F23: 'nothing names this deployment's people, machines or projects' binds every new broker setting and fixture.
findings.answer: Section 5 requires every new setting to carry example names only, following the existing precedent of the broker's service-login map; the repository's own check is one of the named commands, and it was run over the plan itself.

findings.finding: F24: the daemon hands the bearer down at four sites, not one.
findings.answer: Child D names all four: the pane's file and command line (daemon.go:690-699, tmux/spawn.go:175-193), the pod's launch files (manifest.go:259-261, sandbox/launcher.go:414-419), the pruner's special case (daemon/secrets.go:77-80) and the controller command (cmd/legion/controller.go:128-132,304-306).

specDepartures.spec: The cost paragraph says switching the database's identity login on restarts the instance, which takes Dispatch, the secrets broker and every Legion daemon down with it, so it needs its own window and a notice, and that the connection limit may have to be raised in the same window.
specDepartures.plan: No window is asked for and no outage is scheduled. The database slice touches one instance that nothing else depends on, and the plan sizes nothing on the superseded connection figures.
specDepartures.evidence: The flag table for that database product marks its identity-authentication flag as needing no restart and marks the connection limit as needing one; and the architect recorded on 2026-10-25 that the database keeping an agent's conversation is moving to an instance of its own, separate from the one carrying Dispatch, the broker and the Legion daemons.

outcome.scope: The work asks a person for no outage window and schedules none. Any later connection-limit change is a restart of a machine nothing else depends on, and is raised only with a measurement on that new instance.

specDepartures.spec: The exchange 'says which issuer and audience it accepts, whether it requires the token to be bound to that pod, and how the service account's name decides the project and the person', which reads as though one service account could serve several projects.
specDepartures.plan: The service account decides the project one-to-one, and the work includes the deployment naming one worker service account per project in each daemon's configuration file. The exchange carries no project parameter.
specDepartures.evidence: Every pod a daemon launches runs as the one account that daemon's configuration names (packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go:415, packages/daemon/internal/config/kubernetes.go:632-635), each daemon serves exactly one project (packages/daemon/internal/config/config.go:63), and the deployment points every project's daemon at the same shared worker account today.

outcome.scope: One worker service account per project becomes part of the deployment change the Legion slice carries. No Legion code changes for it, and no deployment name enters this repository.
